lessonTitle: Bone and Connective Tissue Disease: Osteoporosis, Fracture Healing and Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

blocks.text: A 72-year-old woman reaches into a low cupboard, feels a sudden pain in her mid-back, and an x-ray shows that a vertebra has collapsed. She has not fallen or been struck. Her bone, silently thinning since the menopause, could no longer carry an ordinary load. A different kind of failure, in a 26-year-old woman with a butterfly rash, joint pain and protein in her urine, shows how the immune system can attack connective tissue throughout the body.

blocks.markdown: Bone is living tissue that is continuously remodelled. **Osteoclasts** resorb bone and **osteoblasts** form it, and they are coupled: osteoblasts and osteocytes express **RANKL**, which binds RANK on osteoclast precursors and drives their activation, while osteoprotegerin (OPG) is a decoy receptor that blocks RANKL. Peak bone mass is reached in early adulthood and then declines with age, so the starting level and the rate of loss together determine fracture risk.

blocks.title: Osteoporosis
blocks.text: Osteoporosis is a skeletal disease of reduced bone mass and disrupted microarchitecture that increases bone fragility and fracture risk. The bone that is present is of normal composition (unlike osteomalacia, where mineralisation is defective). It is defined by bone mineral density (BMD) measurement as a T-score of -2.5 or lower.

blocks.caption: T-score: the number of standard deviations (SD) a patient's bone mineral density lies from the young adult mean (dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry, DXA). Normal is above -1.0, osteopenia -1.0 to -2.5, osteoporosis -2.5 or below.

blocks.title: Calculating a T-score
blocks.prompt: A 66-year-old woman has a femoral neck BMD of 0.62 g/cm^2. The young adult mean is 0.94 g/cm^2 with an SD of 0.12 g/cm^2. Calculate her T-score and classify it.

steps.text: A T-score of -2.67 is below -2.5, so it is in the osteoporotic range.

blocks.markdown:
### Pathogenesis and fracture risk

In **postmenopausal osteoporosis**, loss of oestrogen increases RANKL expression and osteoclast lifespan, so resorption outpaces formation, especially in **trabecular bone**, which has the highest turnover. This predisposes to **vertebral compression fractures** and **distal radius (Colles) fractures**, with **femoral neck fractures** at older ages and cortical thinning. **Senile osteoporosis** reflects age-related decline in osteoblast function. Secondary causes include glucocorticoids, hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, hypogonadism, smoking, alcohol, low calcium and vitamin D, immobility and low body weight. Fracture risk is also raised by falls. Osteoporosis is silent until a fragility fracture occurs, and hip fractures carry considerable morbidity and mortality.

blocks.title: Rate of bone loss
blocks.prompt: A woman's spine BMD falls from 0.94 g/cm^2 to 0.85 g/cm^2 over 5 years. What is the average annual percentage loss?

blocks.markdown:
### Stages of fracture healing

Secondary (indirect) fracture healing proceeds through overlapping stages. First, a **haematoma** forms at the fracture site with an inflammatory phase: platelets and inflammatory cells release cytokines and growth factors over the first days. Second, **soft (fibrocartilaginous) callus** forms as fibroblasts and chondroblasts produce collagen and cartilage, bridging the gap over about 2-3 weeks. Third, **hard (bony) callus** forms as the cartilage is replaced by woven bone through endochondral ossification over weeks to months. Fourth, **remodelling** replaces woven bone with lamellar bone and restores the shape and marrow cavity over months to years, guided by mechanical loading. Healing is impaired by infection, poor blood supply, instability, smoking, diabetes and steroid use.

rows: Clot, platelets, neutrophils and macrophages, cytokine release
Lamellar bone replaces woven bone; contour restored
blocks.caption: Stages of secondary fracture healing (timings are approximate)

blocks.markdown:
### Systemic lupus erythematosus

**Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)** is a chronic autoimmune disease of loss of tolerance to nuclear antigens, mainly in young women (about nine women for each man), with genetic, hormonal and environmental (ultraviolet light, infection) contributions. Autoantibodies form immune complexes that deposit in tissues (a type III hypersensitivity reaction), activate complement and cause inflammation, and some antibodies directly destroy cells (type II). Nearly all patients have **antinuclear antibodies (ANA)**, which are sensitive but not specific; **anti-double-stranded DNA** and **anti-Smith** antibodies are specific; complement levels (C3, C4) fall in active disease.

rows: Malar (butterfly) rash sparing the nasolabial folds, photosensitivity, discoid lesions, oral ulcers
Lupus nephritis (immune complex glomerulonephritis, proteinuria, haematuria)
Antiphospholipid antibodies with thrombosis; fatigue, fever
blocks.caption: Multisystem features of SLE

blocks.title: Common thread
blocks.text: Osteoporosis is a metabolic imbalance of bone turnover, fracture healing is a sequence of repair, and SLE is a systemic autoimmune disease. Fragility fractures, healing stages and autoantibody patterns are each best remembered by their mechanism.

points: Osteoporosis arises when osteoclast resorption exceeds osteoblast formation (oestrogen loss raises RANKL), is defined by a T-score of -2.5 or lower, and causes vertebral, wrist and hip fragility fractures.
Fracture healing proceeds through haematoma and inflammation, soft callus, hard callus and remodelling.
SLE is an immune-complex mediated multisystem disease with malar rash, arthritis, nephritis, serositis, cytopenias and neuropsychiatric features, with ANA, anti-dsDNA and low complement.

questions.stem: Which change in bone remodelling best explains postmenopausal osteoporosis?

options.text: Oestrogen deficiency increases RANKL-driven osteoclast activity so that resorption exceeds formation
Defective mineralisation of osteoid
Excess osteoblast activity producing brittle bone
Failure of osteoclast formation

questions.correctOptionText: Oestrogen deficiency increases RANKL-driven osteoclast activity so that resorption exceeds formation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: loss of oestrogen increases osteoclast formation and survival, so net bone is lost.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: osteoblast activity does not exceed resorption.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: failure of osteoclasts causes osteopetrosis, with dense bone.

questions.explanation: Oestrogen restrains osteoclasts by lowering RANKL signalling. After the menopause, resorption outstrips formation, particularly in trabecular bone, and the microarchitecture is lost.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman on long-term prednisolone has a fragility fracture of the distal radius after tripping on a rug. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Osteoporosis increases fracture risk, which is further raised by glucocorticoid use and falls
Osteoporotic bone is normally mineralised but present in reduced quantity, so falls are not relevant
Glucocorticoids protect against osteoporosis
Wrist fractures are never related to bone density

questions.correctOptionText: Osteoporosis increases fracture risk, which is further raised by glucocorticoid use and falls

distractorRationale.a: Correct: glucocorticoids reduce osteoblast function and bone mass, and falls provide the trauma.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: falls are an important trigger even though the bone is normally mineralised.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: glucocorticoids are a leading secondary cause of osteoporosis.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: distal radius fractures after minimal trauma are typical fragility fractures.

questions.explanation: Fracture risk is a product of bone fragility and the load applied, so both low density and falls matter. Glucocorticoids reduce bone formation and increase resorption.

questions.stem: In which order do the stages of secondary fracture healing occur?

options.text: Haematoma, soft callus, hard callus, remodelling
Hard callus, haematoma, soft callus, remodelling
Remodelling, soft callus, haematoma, hard callus
Soft callus, remodelling, haematoma, hard callus

questions.correctOptionText: Haematoma, soft callus, hard callus, remodelling

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the clot and inflammation come first, then fibrocartilage, woven bone, then remodelling.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: hard callus cannot precede the haematoma.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: remodelling is the final stage.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: soft callus cannot form before the haematoma and inflammatory phase.

questions.explanation: The haematoma supplies cells and signals, fibrocartilage bridges the gap as soft callus, endochondral ossification forms woven bone as hard callus, and remodelling restores lamellar bone.

questions.stem: At 6 weeks after a tibial fracture, a radiograph shows bridging callus consisting mainly of woven bone. Which stage is this?

options.text: Hard (bony) callus formation
Haematoma formation
Soft callus formation
Remodelling to lamellar bone

distractorRationale.a: Correct: woven bone replacing cartilage is the hard callus stage.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: haematoma forms in the first days.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: soft callus is fibrocartilage, not woven bone.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: remodelling replaces woven with lamellar bone later.

questions.explanation: Hard callus consists of woven bone laid down through endochondral ossification, typically over weeks 3-12. Remodelling to lamellar bone follows over months to years.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman has a facial rash across the cheeks sparing the nasolabial folds, arthralgia, pleuritic chest pain, and proteinuria. Which pair of laboratory findings best supports SLE?

options.text: Positive ANA with anti-dsDNA antibodies and low complement
Positive rheumatoid factor with high complement
Negative ANA with raised urate
Positive anti-CCP with erosions

questions.correctOptionText: Positive ANA with anti-dsDNA antibodies and low complement

distractorRationale.a: Correct: ANA is sensitive, anti-dsDNA is specific, and complement is consumed by immune complexes in active disease.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: complement is low, not high, in active SLE.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: ANA is positive in nearly all SLE patients.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: anti-CCP and erosions indicate rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.explanation: SLE is characterised by antinuclear antibodies, with anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith being specific. Immune complexes consume complement, so low C3 and C4 mark activity.

questions.stem: A woman has a lumbar spine BMD of 0.80 g/cm^2. The young adult mean is 1.04 g/cm^2 and the SD is 0.12 g/cm^2. Calculate her T-score.
questions.explanation: T = (0.80 - 1.04) / 0.12 = -0.24 / 0.12 = -2.0. This lies between -1.0 and -2.5, the osteopenic range, not yet osteoporosis by the T-score criterion.

questions.stem: A patient's hip BMD falls from 0.90 g/cm^2 to 0.81 g/cm^2 over 4 years. Calculate the average annual percentage loss of bone density.
questions.explanation: The total fall is 0.09 g/cm^2, which is 10% of 0.90. Over 4 years the average is 2.5% per year, substantially above typical age-related loss and prompting evaluation for causes.

questions.stem: Explain the pathogenesis of postmenopausal osteoporosis and why it leads to vertebral, wrist and hip fractures.
markingGuide: Bone remodelling balance of osteoclast resorption and osteoblast formation
Oestrogen deficiency raises RANKL activity and osteoclast survival
Resorption exceeds formation with loss of trabecular architecture
Trabecular-rich sites (vertebrae, distal radius) and femoral neck are most affected
Reduced strength so low-energy trauma or falls cause fractures
Contributing factors: age, steroids, low calcium and vitamin D, smoking, alcohol, low body weight
questions.explanation: Oestrogen withdrawal tips remodelling towards net loss, and the weakened trabecular architecture fails under ordinary loads. Fracture risk also depends on falls and secondary causes.

questions.stem: Describe the stages of fracture healing and list four factors that impair healing.
markingGuide: Haematoma and inflammation in the first days, with cytokines and growth factors
Soft (fibrocartilaginous) callus over the first weeks
Hard (woven bone) callus by endochondral ossification over weeks to months
Remodelling of woven to lamellar bone over months to years under mechanical load
Impairing factors: infection, poor blood supply, instability or excessive movement, smoking, diabetes, glucocorticoids, poor nutrition
questions.explanation: Healing recapitulates endochondral bone formation in overlapping phases. Anything that interferes with blood supply, stability or cellular activity can delay union or cause non-union.

questions.stem: List the multisystem features of systemic lupus erythematosus, naming the autoantibodies used in diagnosis and explaining the immunological mechanism of tissue damage.
markingGuide: Skin: malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, discoid lesions
Serositis: pleuritis, pericarditis; Libman-Sacks endocarditis; neuropsychiatric disease
ANA sensitive; anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith specific; low complement in active disease
Type III hypersensitivity: immune complex deposition and complement activation; some cytopenias by type II antibody-mediated destruction
questions.explanation: Loss of tolerance to nuclear antigens generates autoantibodies and immune complexes that deposit in many organs, explaining the multisystem presentation. Antibody tests and complement support the diagnosis and monitor activity.
